title: Pinakotheken & Lenbachhaus (Munich): Masterpieces
subtitle: Thirty works across Munich collections, with comparisons that make large changes in painting easier to see.
introduction:
Dürer's frontal self-portrait and Rembrandt's shadowed young face offer two very different degrees of access to a painter. One presents itself with extraordinary clarity; the other allows the features to become difficult to read. Neither approach is simply more realistic. Each decides what a likeness needs to show.

That question widens across this selection. Light can establish a landscape, outlines can give a child weight, and colour can cease to describe what would be seen under ordinary conditions. The later works do not provide an inevitable destination for the earlier ones. They make different choices visible. These paintings and works on paper belong to several Munich collections, so the sequence is for comparison rather than a single walking route.
visitNote: Check the Pinakotheken website before planning a route. The Neue Pinakothek's renovation affects access to its collection, and selected works have been shown at the Alte Pinakothek and Sammlung Schack. Confirm each work's current location with the museum. The Lenbachhaus publishes its own display and visitor information.

books.title: Concerning the Spiritual in Art
books.author: Wassily Kandinsky; translated by M. T. H. Sadler
books.note: Kandinsky's account of colour, form and the aims of painting, in M. T. H. Sadler's English translation. It gives the artist's own arguments to read beside the works selected here, without settling the meaning of every picture.

books.title: Über das Geistige in der Kunst
books.author: Wassily Kandinsky
books.note: Kandinsky's text in German. Read it alongside the English translation when a term or passage deserves closer attention.

books.title: Histoire de Édouard Manet et de son oeuvre
books.author: Théodore Duret
books.note: Duret's early study of Manet, in French. It offers a historical view of the painter whose portrait of Monet appears in this guide; current museum records should be used for dates and attributions.

selectionNote: Artline selected these works from documented museum holdings. The selection is independent of the museum, and individual works may be on loan or off display. Dates and attributions retain the qualifications in the linked records.

works.title: Self-Portrait in a Fur-Trimmed Robe
works.medium: Paint on limewood; binder not specified in source
works.credit: © Bayerische Staatsgemäldesammlungen – Alte Pinakothek München. Albrecht Dürer, Selbstbildnis im Pelzrock, 1500. https://www.sammlung.pinakothek.de/de/artwork/Qlx2QpQ4Xq CC BY-SA 4.0; compressed study reproduction.
works.description: The symmetrical, frontal arrangement recalls images of Christ, a connection the museum makes explicit. Dürer nevertheless preserves the particularity of his own features. The hand touching fur also displays a painter's capacity to distinguish surfaces. Seeing, making and the public dignity of the artist come together in a pose far removed from a casual record of appearance.

works.title: The Crucifixion
works.credit: Giotto di Bondone. The Crucifixion. Image: WikiArt. Public domain (WikiArt label). Proportionally resized and JPEG compressed; no crop.
works.description: The gold setting does not prevent the mourners from having bodily weight. At the foot of the cross they bend, turn and support one another, giving grief several recognisable actions. Giotto connects the figures through those responses rather than making every face repeat one expression. The sacred space remains distinct from ordinary landscape while the gestures remain accessible.

works.title: Saints Cosmas and Damian Saved
works.catalogueTitle: Saint Cosmas and Saint Damian Salvaged
works.credit: Fra Angelico. Saint Cosmas and Saint Damian Salvaged. WikiArt source label: Public domain. Proportional resize and JPEG compression; no crop. Source: https://www.wikiart.org/en/fra-angelico/saint-cosmas-and-saint-damian-salvaged-1440
works.description: The landscape contains more than one moment. Paths, buildings and changes of level separate small groups, allowing the saints' narrative to unfold across a continuous panel. Fra Angelico makes sequence a spatial matter: moving the eye can mean moving forward through events. Each episode retains enough definition to be followed without occupying a separate frame.

works.title: Virgin of the Annunciation
works.credit: Antonello da Messina. Virgin of the Annunciation. Image: WikiArt. Public domain (WikiArt label). Proportionally resized and JPEG compressed; no crop.
works.description: The open book establishes an activity that has been interrupted. Lifted attention and crossed hands provide the response, with little surrounding narrative to explain it. Antonello concentrates the event around face, mantle and gesture. The reduction gives a small alteration in posture the significance that a more crowded Annunciation might distribute among angel, architecture and landscape.

works.title: Madonna of the Curtain
works.credit: Madonna della Tenda. WikiArt; Raphael. Proportional resizing and JPEG compression; source frame preserved.
works.description: The overlapping figures remain distinct because their hands and glances can be followed from one body to another. Raphael's close grouping joins clarity with physical familiarity. The curtain encloses the exchange without interrupting it. An orderly composition is therefore only the starting point: tracing who touches whom reveals a more particular network of attention within the group.

works.title: The Crowning with Thorns
works.credit: Titian. Crowning with Thorns. Image: WikiArt. Public domain (WikiArt label). Proportionally resized and JPEG compressed; no crop.
works.description: Crossing poles and arms press around the seated Christ. Broken boundaries between flesh, cloth and shadow add instability to those competing directions. Titian's handling does not merely fill in a violent arrangement; it participates in its disturbance. Compare the difficulty of settling on an edge here with the readily distinguished bodies in Raphael's nearby selection entry.

works.title: The Great Last Judgement
works.medium: Paint on canvas; binder not specified in source
works.credit: © Bayerische Staatsgemäldesammlungen – Alte Pinakothek München. Peter Paul Rubens, Das Große Jüngste Gericht, um 1617. https://www.sammlung.pinakothek.de/de/artwork/Dj4mkQbL5A CC BY-SA 4.0; compressed study reproduction.
works.description: The crowd becomes intelligible through large movements of rising and falling bodies. Light separates passages that would be difficult to read as individual figures from a distance. Rubens organises the altarpiece at more than one scale: broad directions first, particular limbs and faces later. A small reproduction can explain this design but cannot reproduce the physical encounter with its size.

works.title: The Hippopotamus and Crocodile Hunt
works.credit: Peter Paul Rubens. Hippopotamus and Crocodile Hunt. Image: WikiArt. Public domain (WikiArt label). Proportionally resized and JPEG compressed; no crop.
works.description: Horses, hunters and animals press into a shared centre with little space to retreat. Weapons and limbs pull against one another, while contrasting hides, flesh and clothes keep parts of the struggle identifiable. The hunt is constructed as a spectacle of collision. Its compressed arrangement tells more about Rubens's pictorial decisions than about how the animals behave outside a painting.

works.title: The Risen Christ
works.credit: Rembrandt van Rijn. Christ Resurrected. Image: WikiArt. Public domain (WikiArt label). Proportionally resized and JPEG compressed; no crop.
works.description: The lit torso and nearby hand give the half-length figure the proximity of a portrait. The museum identifies Christ after the Resurrection, presented without the visible wounds of the Passion. Little surrounding action explains the event. Instead, the frontal encounter lets a religious image address the viewer through the same close attention that a portrait can establish.

works.title: Self-Portrait as a Young Man
works.medium: Paint on oak; binder not specified in source
works.credit: © Bayerische Staatsgemäldesammlungen – Alte Pinakothek München. Rembrandt (Harmensz. van Rijn), Jugendliches Selbstbildnis, 1629. https://www.sammlung.pinakothek.de/de/artwork/y7GE1PmGPV CC BY-SA 4.0; compressed study reproduction.
works.description: Rembrandt gives the viewer less of his face than the light might initially promise. Hair casts shadow over the features while a collar and curls catch brighter accents. Likeness has to survive that uneven access. Beside Dürer's explicit frontal presentation, the painting makes concealment an active part of self-portraiture rather than merely a lack of illumination.

works.title: Sunflowers
works.credit: © Bayerische Staatsgemäldesammlungen – Neue Pinakothek München. Vincent van Gogh, Sonnenblumen, 1888. https://www.sammlung.pinakothek.de/de/artwork/Y0GR9B7LRX CC BY-SA 4.0; compressed study reproduction.
works.description: Yellow repeats without producing identical flowers. Open blooms, curling petals and heavy seed heads supply different shapes within the restricted range. The blue-green background belongs to this Munich version and helps distinguish it from others in the series. Each head changes the balance of the group through its stage, direction and density, not simply through a different colour.

works.title: Monet in His Studio Boat
works.credit: Édouard Manet. Monet in his Studio Boat. WikiArt source label: Public domain. Proportional resize and JPEG compression; no crop. Source: https://www.wikiart.org/en/edouard-manet/monet-in-his-floating-studio-1874
works.description: The boat places the painter inside the conditions he is painting. Its dark shelter frames pale clothes and an easel while broken marks describe the surrounding water. Manet's portrait makes an outdoor working arrangement visible. The finished landscape is no longer the only subject; the means of observing and producing it have acquired their own place in the image.

works.title: The Poor Poet
works.credit: Carl Spitzweg. The Poor Poet. Image: WikiArt. Public domain (WikiArt label). Proportionally resized and JPEG compressed; no crop.
works.description: An umbrella has become indoor equipment. Its shelter above the attic bed gives the room's literary activity an inconveniently practical context, reinforced by books, papers and the low ceiling. Spitzweg's comedy depends on those material conditions rather than on a grand claim about genius. The Munich version is dated 1839 in its collection record.

works.title: The Gazebo
works.credit: The Gazebo. WikiArt; Caspar David Friedrich. Proportional resizing and JPEG compression; source frame preserved.
works.description: The distant spire reaches the viewer through a sheltered opening of plants and supports. Friedrich includes the place from which the view is seen, with two figures pausing inside it. The enclosure gives distance a frame and a bodily starting point. Landscape becomes an act of looking from somewhere particular rather than an unrestricted prospect.

works.title: Christ and the Samaritan Woman at the Well
works.catalogueTitle: Christ and the Samaritan woman at the well
works.credit: Angelica Kauffman. Christ and the Samaritan woman at the well. Image: WikiArt. Public domain (WikiArt label). Proportionally resized and JPEG compressed; no crop.
works.description: The two figures' hands divide the exchange into gestures that can be followed across the well. Red and blue keep the bodies clearly separate against a restrained landscape. Kauffman gives conversation the structure of an event without surrounding it with a crowd. Direction, distance and response provide enough action for the biblical encounter.

works.title: A Beer Garden in Munich
works.credit: Max Liebermann. Beer Garden in Munich. Image: WikiArt. Public domain (WikiArt label). Proportionally resized and JPEG compressed; no crop.
works.description: Tree trunks repeatedly interrupt the view of tables and visitors. Moving between them reveals partial encounters rather than one dominant incident. Sunlight supplies further breaks across clothing and ground. Liebermann lets a public gathering remain dispersed: the picture's breadth comes from many simultaneous occupations, not from assembling every face around a central protagonist.

works.title: Children with a Goldfish Bowl
works.credit: Paula Modersohn-Becker. Children with goldfish bowl. WikiArt source label: Public domain. Proportional resize and JPEG compression; no crop. Source: https://www.wikiart.org/en/paula-modersohn-becker/children-with-goldfish-bowl-1907
works.description: The held bowl keeps attention close to the child's body, which is defined through broad shapes and firm boundaries. Leaves and objects crowd the narrow field without dissolving that weight. Modersohn-Becker's simplified modelling differs from Liebermann's interrupted light. The comparison shows two means of establishing a figure: an accumulating silhouette and a shifting set of illuminated parts.

works.title: A Street in Upper Norwood
works.credit: © Bayerische Staatsgemäldesammlungen – Neue Pinakothek München. Camille Pissarro, Straße in Upper Norwood, 1871. https://www.sammlung.pinakothek.de/de/artwork/PdxzrBExw5 CC BY-SA 4.0; compressed study reproduction.
works.description: The road and rooflines supply a direction beneath the broad grey sky. Small walkers fit into that recession, while bare branches interrupt it. Pissarro asks an ordinary suburban street to carry the work of a landscape. Its recognisable structure gives depth without a dramatic landmark, allowing houses and everyday movement to remain sufficient subjects.

works.title: The Road to Hampton Court
works.credit: Alfred Sisley. The Road to Hampton Court. Image credit: Alfred Sisley. Wikimedia Commons. Public domain (https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/mark/1.0/). Resized and JPEG-compressed; selected source frame preserved.
works.description: The warm path draws the view into the distance beside cooler water. Trees and figures repeat at changing sizes, making that recession measurable. Unlike the enclosed Norwood street, the river leaves one side open. Sisley uses the same basic device, a route leading away, to produce a more expansive relation between the near ground and the sky.

works.title: Dance Around the Golden Calf
works.credit: Emil Nolde. Dance Around the Golden Calf. Image: WikiArt. Public domain (WikiArt label). Proportionally resized and JPEG compressed; no crop.
works.description: Stretched limbs alternately merge with colour and reappear at emphatic boundaries. The dance's agitation therefore continues beyond the bodies into the painted surface. Nolde's yellow, red and blue need not imitate ordinary illumination to organise the scene. Their abrupt contacts make movement available even where a particular pose becomes difficult to separate from its setting.

works.title: Blue Horse I
works.credit: Franz Marc. Blue Horse I. Image: WikiArt. Public domain (WikiArt label). Proportionally resized and JPEG compressed; no crop.
works.description: The lowered head remains recognisably equine despite the horse's blue. Rounded hills repeat the curve of its neck, joining animal and landscape through shape rather than naturalistic colour. Marc allows familiarity and alteration to coexist. The body supplies enough identification for colour to take on a different compositional role without making the subject disappear.
works.museum: Städtische Galerie im Lenbachhaus und Kunstbau München

works.title: Colour Study: Squares with Concentric Circles
works.catalogueTitle: Color Study: Squares with Concentric Circles
works.credit: Wassily Kandinsky. Color Study: Squares with Concentric Circles. Image: WikiArt. Public domain (WikiArt label). Proportionally resized and JPEG compressed; no crop.
works.description: Each square changes the neighbours around its rings. Width, order and proportion vary, so a colour's apparent force can be compared under different conditions. Kandinsky gives the study no hidden figurative subject to solve. Its work happens in the comparisons themselves, through repeated forms that remain deliberately irregular enough to avoid becoming a mechanical chart.
works.museum: Städtische Galerie im Lenbachhaus und Kunstbau München

works.title: Into the Night
works.credit: Marianne von Werefkin. Into the night. Image: WikiArt. Public domain (WikiArt label). Proportionally resized and JPEG compressed; no crop.
works.description: Close façades narrow the walkers' passage, leaving little sky above. Blue, red and violet intensify the separation of buildings and clothes within that enclosure. Werefkin makes pressure a visible property of the street's proportions. The figures' private thoughts remain unknown; the surrounding architecture already explains why the space can feel difficult to move through.
works.museum: Städtische Galerie im Lenbachhaus und Kunstbau München

works.title: Jawlensky and Werefkin
works.credit: Gabriele Münter. Jawlensky and Werefkin. Image: WikiArt. Public domain (WikiArt label). Proportionally resized and JPEG compressed; no crop.
works.description: The green slope tilts the resting artists toward the picture's surface. Their clothes form distinct patches beneath the broad blue sky, allowing portrait likeness and landscape design to coexist. Münter gives the sitters individual poses without withdrawing them from the larger colour arrangement. The ground is as consequential to the portrait as either figure's position upon it.
works.museum: Städtische Galerie im Lenbachhaus und Kunstbau München

works.title: Kandinsky and Erma Bossi at the Table in the Murnau House
works.catalogueTitle: Kandinsky and Erma Bossi at the Table in the Murnau House
works.credit: Gabriele Münter. Kandinsky and Erma Bossi at the Table in the Murnau House. Image: WikiArt. Public domain (WikiArt label). Proportionally resized and JPEG compressed; no crop.
works.description: A pale tablecloth and faces emerge against the dark wall, with chairs and small objects establishing a particular room. Münter gives an artistic association the setting of ordinary domestic company. The large colour blocks keep the encounter compact. No ceremonial pose is needed for the gathering to become a record of people sharing a working circle's everyday world.
works.museum: Städtische Galerie im Lenbachhaus und Kunstbau München

works.title: Portrait of the Dancer Alexander Sakharoff
works.catalogueTitle: Portrait of the Dancer Alexander Sakharoff
works.credit: Alexej von Jawlensky. Portrait of the Dancer Alexander Sakharoff. Image: WikiArt. Public domain (WikiArt label). Proportionally resized and JPEG compressed; no crop.
works.description: The red costume gathers the body into one forceful area beneath a pale, made-up face. Its turn differs from the outward gaze, preventing the portrait from becoming entirely frontal. Jawlensky makes stage appearance inseparable from the sitter's identity. Hair, eyes and mouth acquire their intensity through the surrounding colour rather than through an extensively described performance setting.
works.museum: Städtische Galerie im Lenbachhaus und Kunstbau München

works.title: Promenade
works.credit: August Macke. Promenade. Image: WikiArt. Public domain (WikiArt label). Proportionally resized and JPEG compressed; no crop.
works.description: Upright bodies continue a pattern begun by tree trunks. Clothing and changes of direction keep the walkers identifiable within broad interlocking foliage. Macke connects public leisure to a close arrangement of forms, making people and vegetation routes through the same surface. Following the scene's activity and following its design need not be two separate operations.
works.museum: Städtische Galerie im Lenbachhaus und Kunstbau München

works.title: Murnau View with Railway and Castle
works.catalogueTitle: Murnau view with railway and castle
works.credit: Wassily Kandinsky. Murnau view with railway and castle. WikiArt source label: Public domain. Proportional resize and JPEG compression; no crop. Source: https://www.wikiart.org/en/wassily-kandinsky/murnau-view-with-railway-and-castle-1909
works.description: The train supplies a firm horizontal beneath bright, angular land and sky. Enough locomotive, pole and building remains for a place to be recognised, even as colour gains greater independence. That stable lower line helps hold the fragments together. The painting offers a useful comparison with *Improvisation: Gorge*, where such dependable coordinates become much harder to find.
works.museum: Städtische Galerie im Lenbachhaus und Kunstbau München

works.title: Self-Portrait with a Skeleton
works.credit: Lovis Corinth. Self-portrait with Skeleton. Image: WikiArt. Public domain (WikiArt label). Proportionally resized and JPEG compressed; no crop.
works.description: The skeleton and the clothed painter occupy comparable amounts of studio space. As an object of study, the bones belong to the room; as a counterpart to Corinth's living body, they also make mortality available as a reading. The comparison requires little additional symbolism. Two upright figures before the windows are enough to establish it.
works.museum: Städtische Galerie im Lenbachhaus und Kunstbau München

works.title: Improvisation: Gorge
works.credit: Wassily Kandinsky. Improvisation. Gorge. WikiArt source label: Public domain. Proportional resize and JPEG compression; no crop. Source: https://www.wikiart.org/en/wassily-kandinsky/improvisation-gorge-1914
works.description: The title suggests terrain, but lines and colours do not settle into a single surveyable place. Diagonals may imply a slope, then continue across boundaries that interrupt a consistent view. Kandinsky allows those elements to act beyond the job of describing objects. The comparison with the railway landscape makes their increased independence concrete rather than merely calling the work abstract.
works.museum: Städtische Galerie im Lenbachhaus und Kunstbau München

closingSections.title: Plan by collection, look by comparison
paragraphs: Choose the pair that interests you, then check which institution holds each work and whether it is currently displayed. The Pinakothek collections and Lenbachhaus are not a single venue. Works on paper in particular may rotate; an online collection record is a starting point for planning, not a promise of permanent access.
